newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Belgrade don refuses to resign, angers students.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade don refuses to resign, angers students.

text.p: Belgrade University rector Dragutin Velickovic on Tuesday angered thousands of Serbian students who have been protesting for 103 days, when he refused to bow to their demands and resign.
Speaking at a news conference he instead asked for the dismissal of all faculty deans and institute chiefs who have supported the daily student protest.

This provoked cries of "shame on you" from the attending students who the rector then threw out of the room. They were outraged with Velickovic's remarks and said they would radicalise their otherwise peaceful protests.

"The whole thing is another of Velickovic's sick jokes," student protest spokesman Dusan Vasiljevic said. "The students will not go back to classes because in their view the rector has already been replaced."

The student protests continued even after the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition ended its record three-month demonstrations in February, after Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic restored local election victories in 14 cities which his ruling socialist party (SPS) annulled in November.
The widespread protests were the biggest challenge to Milosevic's 10-year rule and ended 52 years of communist control of the capital Belgrade when Zajedno leader Zoran Djindjic took over as mayor.
The students however carried on marching, demanding the resignation of the rector, a die-hard SPS appointee who condemned their demonstrations as siding with his political foes.
Protest organisers said there were plans for the students to march to the rector's office on Wednesday and throw his belongings out into the street.
Minutes later, scores of students crashed a cocktail given for the press by Rada Milentijevic, a Milosevic loyalist recently appointed as Serbian information minister, in the nearby National Museum.
They barged among bewildered and embarrassed officials and domestic and foreign journalists blowing their customary whistles and trumpets and chanting "Red Gang".

Velickovic's move on Tuesday followed a meeting of the Belgrade University Teaching Board on Sunday when 27 faculty deans (out of a total of 30) and chiefs of all eight institutes sided with the students and voted for Velickovic's dismissal.
They elected Dragan Kuburovic as the new university chief in a move Velickovic proclaimed as illegal.
Velickovic's initiative for sacking the rebel deans will be discussed at the University Council which meets when called by Milosevic's government.
Velickovic has refused to budge from his post despite a written agreement by two Serbian deputy prime ministers last December that he would be sacked.
He promised to resign only when the students returned to their classes -- a move they refuse to do.
All opposition leaders and sympathisers have backed the student protests.
"The student protests are the most important struggle for democracy in the past 50 years," former Belgrade Mayor Nebojsa Covic recently said in a television show.

Zajedno was preparing fresh protests for Saturday, the 6th anniversary of massive anti-government demonstrations in Belgrade in which two people were killed. Milosevic sent tanks into the streets to quell the opposition.
